title: Drought, intense heat worsens drinking water shortage in several villages of Manapparai - The Hindu

full_text:
Collecting potable water has become a daily battle for the residents of Manapparai and surrounding villages.
| Photo Credit: FILE PHOTO
Intense summer has triggered an acute drinking water shortage for people of Manapparai,Vaiyampatti, and neighbouring villages in Tiruchi district.
Manapparai is a rain shadow region in the district. While farmers largely depend on seasonal rainfall for the crops, they depend upon the Cauvery water for drinking, which is supplied under various combined water schemes. The region generally faces water crisis in summer.
Several villages of Manapparai, Vaiyampatti, and Marungapuri blocks witnessed drinking water shortage in summer. The problem began to surface in February and intensified since after the onset of summer. Normally, the problem would ease a bit with the end of summer. But the continued spell of summer-like weather has worsened the water scarcity.
According to sources, drinking water scarcity was reported in at least 40 to 50 villages in Manapparai region. In Manapparai, the residents now get drinking water once in three or four days. The residents of several villages around Manapparai complain of erratic supply. They are supplied with water once a week. Since the supply was erratic, they depend on borewells and open wells for their daily needs. This too has become difficult as the groundwater level has been sinking drastically due to the drought.
Villages such as Aniyapur, Sandhaipettai, Kuppanampatti, Kattayampatti, Veeramalaipalayam, Nallampillai, Udayarpatti, Balakulathupatti, and Veerappur were under the grip of acute shortage of drinking water.
“We get Cauvery water once a week. It is supplied only for a few minutes. No one gets more than two pots of water. It is not sufficient even for a day’s use. Moreover, the supply is erratic and we do not know when water is supplied,” says Nagaraj, a resident of Veerappur near Aniyapur.
A senior official told The Hindu that water yield at the source points of combined water schemes had come down because of the failure of monsoon. The situation had to be largely maintained by tapping the local water resources. The officials of the District Rural Development Agency had been given instruction to focus on drinking water supply. Intervention activities such as sinking additional borewells and augmenting water sources in villages had been undertaken where the issues had cropped up. Water supply would be the priority of officials until the onset of northeast monsoon.

full_text:
Internally displaced Palestinian families in southern Gaza are enduring extreme summer heat inside worn-out tents without cooling equipment, using makeshift methods to cope with daytime temperatures.
Some families cover tents to block direct sunlight and open shelters for airflow, while others spray children with water for heat relief.
About 1.9 million of Gaza’s 2.4 million residents live in tents and temporary shelters after Israel destroyed their homes in its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip, which began in October 2023.
The genocide has killed more than 73,400 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 others, with 90% of civilian infrastructure damaged or destroyed, Gaza Health Ministry figures show. The U.N. has estimated reconstruction costs at about $70 billion.
Survival ‘nearly impossible’
Jamalat Siam, a displaced Palestinian from Rafah in southern Gaza, lives in a tent in the al-Mawasi area west of Khan Younis.
She said rising temperatures have made staying inside the tent "nearly impossible” due to the lack of cooling equipment.
"In the summer, we cannot sit inside the tent. We put a barrier over it and stay in the shade,” she told Turkish Anadolu Agency (AA).
She said children are particularly affected by the heat, pouring water over themselves to cool down, sometimes resulting in exhaustion.
Rubble barrier
Beyond combating heat, piles of rubble scattered around displacement areas have become barriers some families use to block sunlight and protect themselves from Israeli gunfire.
Siam said her family collects rubble from streets and destroyed homes to place around their tents.
The barriers provide little security. Siam said her area "is not safe," and residents fear an Israeli ground incursion at any time.
Water scarcity
The water crisis further burdens displaced families forced to travel long distances to reach water sources, especially drinking water.
Kholoud Abu Mohsen, a mother of five from Khan Younis, told AA her family must travel long distances for daily water.
Abu Mohsen places her children in a plastic basin with water to relieve intense heat, but difficulty obtaining water forces her to ration it.
She said the extreme heat has worsened her family’s suffering, even with openings she made in their shelter above their destroyed home’s ruins to improve ventilation.
Her efforts have failed to ease the heat. Pieces of cardboard and plastic substitute for electric fans amid an electricity crisis persisting since Israel’s genocidal war began about three years ago.
The family also struggles to secure food and relies primarily on rice and lentils. One of Abu Mohsen’s daughters has a congenital eye condition that requires treatment, while her about 6-month-old daughter suffers from severe malnutrition.
Abu Mohsen said living conditions force her to work daily for meager wages of five or 10 shekels ($1.70 or $3.30) to buy diapers and other essential supplies.
Despite a cease-fire agreement reached on Oct. 10, 2025, Israel continues its blockade of the Gaza Strip, imposing strict restrictions on the movement of people, goods and aid, and continuing military operations that have killed more than 1,270 Palestinians and injured over 4,420 others, most of them women and children, Gaza Health Ministry figures show.
On Aug. 22, 2025, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification Global Initiative announced in a report that "famine was occurring in Gaza City” in the northern Gaza Strip.

title: Will there be another heatwave in September? Here’s what we know - The Independent

full_text:
Heavy downpours and flash flooding were predicted for parts of the UK this week, before drier conditions return over the weekend.
The rain and cooler temperatures were welcomed after back-to-back heatwaves left the ground hard and dry with 70 per cent of England and Wales in drought.
Provisional Met Office data shows that the UK’s mean temperature for meteorological summer so far is currently at 16.48C – that is 1.88C above the 1991 to 2020 average temperature. England has recorded a mean summer temperature of 18.19C so far, 2.46C above average.
The remainder of August would need to be 1.41C below the summer average for England to equal its current warmest summer on record, also set in 2025.
But will there be another dry and sunny spell this summer?
What does the long range forecast say?
Looking ahead, the Met Office’s long range weather forecast predicts that the changeable weather is likely to continue.
From early next week the south of England is forecast to see more unsettled weather as longer spells of rain spread north across many parts of the UK.
In the days before the start of September some heavy bursts and thunderstorms are likely.
“Thereafter, it will likely remain changeable through the rest of August and into early September, with rainfall amounts probably above average for the time of year,” according to the Met Office.
But warm and hot spells are still possible, although they will likely be short lived, with temperatures sitting near average.
There will be some drier and more settled spells before an unsettled start to autumn.
At the start of September the Met Office predicts all areas will probably see a mixture of showers and dry weather.
While the beginning of September will bring varying temperatures by mid-September, there may be an increase in the extent of drier, more settled weather, especially in the south and east, according to forecasters.
What records have been broken this summer?
The Met Office said last week temperatures had reached 37.6C at Charlwood in Surrey, while at Wisley temperatures had hit 37.2C, and Kew Gardens in London had recorded a temperature of 38.1C – the highest temperature recorded in the UK this year.
A further 10 weather stations were at or above 36C, the provisional figures from the Met Office showed.
It makes 2026 the first year on record to see three separate days where temperatures reached the 37C threshold, as well as the first year with four days at 36C or above.
Before 2026, the UK had recorded 37C or higher on only six occasions.
It also extends 2026’s record-breaking run of days above 35C.
For four months in a row temperatures hit 35C in the UK on at least one day in May, June, July and now August.
July was also the driest month since records began in 1836 in both England and Wales, southern England alone had its driest calendar month ever on record.
By 15 July this year the UK had already recorded more days above 30C than in the whole of 1976, which was known for its long-lasting heatwave.
Why is the UK experiencing more heatwaves?
Climate change is making extremes such as heat and drought more intense and more likely.
The UK's weather is becoming warmer and wetter, and adverse weather events - heatwaves, flooding, extreme cold - are growing more frequent and intense. The last decade has been warmer than any previous decade on record, and summers we once considered exceptional are becoming the norm.
The Met Office explains that the UK is experiencing higher maximum temperatures and longer warm spells in recent years. Warm spells have seen their average length more than double – increasing from 5.3 days in 1961-90 to over 13 days in the decade 2008-2017.
But the outlook could get worse. A study by the Met Office Hadley Centre suggests the current chance of seeing days reaching 40C or more is extremely low. However, by 2100 under a high emissions scenario the UK could see 40 C days every three to four years.

title: 7 post-heatwave jobs to tackle before the rain hits, to help prevent damp, damage and mess - Good Housekeeping

full_text:
That’s right, rain is finally on the way. For what seems like the first time in an eternity, weather forecasters are predicting showers across the UK in the coming week. It certainly feels strangely out of character for Brits to be wishing for rain, a phenomenon we’re more than a little accustomed to, but after months of drought and hosepipe bans up and down the country, it’s safe to say we’re ready for more than a drizzle. Or are we?
After one of the hottest and driest summers on record, our homes have certainly felt the effects. From changes to our buildings and gardens to the everyday habits we’ve adopted to cope with the heat, we’ve all become surprisingly accustomed to long spells of hot, dry weather – which means we might not be quite as prepared for the rain as we think.
From prepping your garden so the rainfall actually benefits it to adjusting your household habits to avoid excess moisture, damp and humidity indoors, these are the mistakes to avoid around your home when the rain returns.
Expecting rain to fix the drought
Getty Images
As much as I, too, want to see all of our scorched earth return to its once green and luscious self, a brief spell of rain won’t immediately undo the damage caused by weeks of drought.
When soil becomes very dry and compacted, rain can struggle to soak in properly and may simply run off the surface instead of reaching the roots below. So, while a downpour might make the garden look refreshed, it doesn’t necessarily mean your plants are suddenly getting all the water they need.
Rather than assuming the rain has done the job for you, check the soil a few centimetres below the surface once the shower has passed. If it still feels dry, your garden may need a little more help – although, of course, you should always check whether any local water restrictions are still in place.
Adding a layer of mulch can also help the soil hold on to moisture for longer, making the most of any much-needed rainfall that does arrive.
Drying wet clothes inside
When the rain returns, so too does the dreaded indoor clothes airer. But moving wet washing inside without changing how you dry it can quickly add extra moisture to the air, increasing the risk of condensation, damp and mould.
Try to dry clothes in a well-ventilated room, keep them spaced out rather than packed tightly together and use an extractor fan or dehumidifier if you have one. An extra spin cycle before hanging clothes up can also help remove more water and speed up drying.
Most importantly, avoid draping wet washing over radiators or leaving several loads to dry in a closed room. The quicker you can get that moisture out of the fabric and out of the house, the better.

Assuming water restrictions are over
Getty Images
A few days of rain might have you reaching for the hosepipe again, but don’t assume the restrictions we’ve become accustomed to this summer have disappeared along with the sunshine.
Despite the wetter forecast, water supplies remain under significant pressure after such a prolonged dry spell. The latest Environment Agency update says reservoir storage across England has fallen to 69%, around 11.6% below the long-term average, while more than 25 million people are currently affected by water-use restrictions.
The Met Office has also stressed just how dry this summer has been, with the lack of rainfall contributing directly to pressure on water resources and the introduction of hosepipe restrictions in parts of England.
So, even if your garden is getting a much-needed soaking, check with your local water company before using a hosepipe, pressure washer or sprinkler. Government advice is clear that restrictions vary by area and your water provider is the best place to check the rules that apply to you.
Closing all the windows
If you’re anything like me, I can’t remember the last time I closed my windows, thanks to the relentless heatwave leaving me desperate for just the hint of a gust of wind. But with rain on the way, many of us may see this an opportunity to finally close up shop – it’s not.
After weeks of trying to keep the heat out, it can be tempting to shut every window as soon as the rain arrives. But keeping your home completely sealed can trap moisture inside, especially when you’re cooking, showering or drying clothes indoors.
You don’t need to leave windows wide open while it’s pouring, but it’s still important to keep air moving. Use extractor fans, keep trickle vents open if you have them and air rooms whenever the weather allows.
A little ventilation goes a long way in helping prevent condensation from settling on windows and walls, which can eventually lead to damp and mould.
Storing wet items
Getty Images
Brollies and raincoats may start being worked back into rotation soon and a common mistake I always see friends and family making is not thinking twice about how you store these items. Rainy weather inevitably means wetter shoes, coats, umbrellas and bags coming back into the house, but try not to shove them straight into cupboards, baskets or enclosed storage while they’re still damp.
Moisture trapped in dark, poorly ventilated spaces can quickly lead to musty smells, mildew and, in some cases, mould. Instead, give wet items time to dry properly first – hang coats somewhere with good airflow, leave umbrellas open to dry and avoid piling damp shoes together in a closed cabinet.
It’s a small habit change, but one that can make a big difference, especially when you remember this rainy period is set to end in September. With yet another heatwave on the horizon, high temperatures will only make processes (and smells) such as this worse.
Not checking the gutters and drains
After weeks of dry weather, checking your gutters and drains probably hasn’t been high on the to-do list. But the first heavy spell of rain can quickly reveal any blockages that have been quietly building up over summer.
Dust, moss, leaves and other debris can stop water flowing away properly, causing gutters to overflow or water to collect around the outside of your home. In turn, that can increase the risk of damp, leaks, water damage and even pests like rats. Yikes!
Before the rain gets too heavy, check any drains and gullies you can safely access from ground level and clear away obvious debris. It’s also worth keeping an eye on your gutters during a downpour – if water is spilling over the sides or running down the exterior wall, it could be a sign they need clearing.
Forgetting the furniture
Getty Images
After weeks of hot, dry weather, your garden furniture has probably spent more time uncovered than usual and no doubt more in use than ever before. But with the return of rain, it may need a little more tender love and care than you realise.
Avoid leaving cushions, parasols and other soft furnishings outside to repeatedly get soaked, as trapped moisture can lead to mildew, mould and unpleasant smells. If they do get caught in a shower, let them dry completely before storing them away.
Wooden furniture is also worth checking after a long spell of heat, as prolonged sun can leave it dry and weathered. Once the rain passes, give it time to dry properly before applying any oils, stains or protective treatments, otherwise you risk trapping moisture underneath. Whichever way the weather turns, make sure to do this before storing anything away for the autumn.

PSG moves opening Ligue 1 match after heatwave damages pitch
The match, scheduled for Sunday (23 August), will now be played at Rennes’ stadium.
Paris Saint-Germain has moved its opening French league match of the season against Rennes to Rennes after a summer heatwave badly damaged the pitch at Parc des Princes.
The match, scheduled for Sunday (23 August), will now be played at Rennes' stadium, the French soccer competitions committee announced late Wednesday (19 August).
PSG said the condition of its home pitch had deteriorated so badly that the game could not be played there safely or under suitable conditions for the players.
The club said the venue change was agreed with Rennes and thanked the club for helping make the match possible.
"Paris Saint-Germain fully understands the inconvenience caused by this change for its supporters and all those who had planned to attend this match at the Parc des Princes," the club said, adding that it regretted the unusual situation.
PSG said it had already found a solution to replace the damaged pitch at Parc des Princes. The new surface is expected to be ready for the club's next home Ligue 1 match against Monaco on Sept. 4.
